body:
2.2.2 currently distinguishes between "weak" authenticators, such as e-mail which cannot be used and "restricted" authenticators (such as SMS) which can be used only if stronger ones are available as well. 

What is the reason why e-mail is considered weaker than SMS (or VoIP is worse than PSTN)?

The stipulation is also rather restrictive when typical password reset mechanisms are considered ("forgot password"). Most online services (that do not enforce 2 factor authentication) send password reset links via e-mail. Therefore, an attacker could use this mechanism as an alternative to needing the password. I would in this case consider it an "authenticator".

Since many typical applications use such a password reset mechanism, there is a bit of a disconnect between ASVS and real-world applications. To resolve this we could either

a) provide some guidance on how a better password reset mechanism can be implemented realistically for at least ASVS Level 1 applications. I cannot think of any practical way to implement this for many online services. 
b) do not enforce the stipulation for at least level 1.
c) clarify that password reset is not considered here.

I suggest these reasons why email is weak.

- emails are not required to be encrypted during transfer, that any middle servers can get the contents.
- emails in inbox are managed by each service provider, that means, there is no guarantee that administrators or support operators don't watch the emails.
- SMS on the phone is bound to the device, but email account is not, that makes the door to the email account open to the internet. (but I think it is the same risk as SSO.)

You can choose methods for password reset among NIST's list, such as time-based OTP, OTP via mobile push channel, look-up secrets. If you cannot control risks, maybe you choose an operational way instead of automatic recovery.
I opened a PR on #1394 and opened #1447 to deal with the "weak authenticators" question so closing this for now.
